:::{#thm-pearson-cosine-centered}
#### Pearson correlation is the cosine similarity of the centered vectors

Let $\vx, \vy \in \reals^n$ be two vectors that are not constant,
with means $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sumin x_i$ and $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sumin y_i$.
Write $\cent{\vx} = \vx - \bar{x}\,\vone$ and $\cent{\vy} = \vy - \bar{y}\,\vone$
for the **centered** vectors, whose means are zero.
Then the [Pearson correlation coefficient](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/exploratory-descriptive.html#def-pearson-r) $r$
of the $n$ pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ is the cosine similarity (@def-cosine-similarity) of the centered vectors:

$$
r = \cossim(\cent{\vx}, \cent{\vy}).
$$

:::

::: proof

Entry $i$ of $\cent{\vx}$ is $x_i - \bar{x}$, and entry $i$ of $\cent{\vy}$ is $y_i - \bar{y}$.
Neither centered vector is zero, because neither $\vx$ nor $\vy$ is constant, so the cosine similarity is defined.
The three pieces of the cosine similarity are

$$
\ba
\cent{\vx} \cdot \cent{\vy} &= \sumin (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}), \\
\norm{\cent{\vx}} &= \sqrt{\sumin (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \\
\norm{\cent{\vy}} &= \sqrt{\sumin (y_i - \bar{y})^2},
\ea
$$

by the definitions of the dot product and the Euclidean norm.
Dividing the first by the product of the other two gives the formula for $r$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-pearson-cosine-centered}
#### Centering changes the cosine similarity

Take $\vx = (1, 2, 3)$ and $\vy = (1, 3, 2)$.
Their means are $\bar{x} = \bar{y} = 2$, so $\cent{\vx} = (-1, 0, 1)$ and $\cent{\vy} = (-1, 1, 0)$.
Then

$$
\ba
\cent{\vx} \cdot \cent{\vy} &= 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, \\
\norm{\cent{\vx}} &= \norm{\cent{\vy}} = \sqrt{2},
\ea
$$

so $r = \cossim(\cent{\vx}, \cent{\vy}) = 1 / 2$.

Without centering, $\vx \cdot \vy = 1 + 6 + 6 = 13$ and $\norm{\vx} = \norm{\vy} = \sqrt{14}$,
so $\cossim(\vx, \vy) = 13 / 14$.
The uncentered value is close to $1$ mostly because both vectors have positive entries and the same mean, not because they move together.

:::
